content: Granulation tissue is a type of vascularized, fibrous connective tissue that replaces the fibrin clot in healing wounds. It typically originates from the base of a wound and has the capacity to fill wounds of nearly any size. The herb chamomile has been suggested to promote the growth of granulation tissue. During the proliferative phase of wound healing, granulation tissue exhibits specific characteristics. It appears light red or dark pink due to the presence of newly formed capillary loops or buds. It is soft to the touch, moist, and has a bumpy or granular texture. The structure of granulation tissue is composed of a tissue matrix that supports various cell types, each associated with one of three primary functions: extracellular matrix formation, immune response, or vascularization. The extracellular matrix of granulation tissue is synthesized and modified by fibroblasts. Initially, it consists of a network of Type III collagen, a weaker form of structural protein that can be produced rapidly. Over time, this is replaced by the stronger, long-stranded Type I collagen, which is characteristic of scar tissue. The immune system plays a critical role in granulation tissue. The primary immune cells active in this tissue are macrophages and neutrophils, although other leukocytes are also present. These cells function to phagocytize old or damaged tissue and protect the healing tissue from pathogenic insults. This immune activity is essential for both facilitating the healing process and defending against invading pathogens, as the wound often lacks an effective skin barrier to serve as a first line of defense. Vascularization, or angiogenesis, is crucial for the development of granulation tissue. A network of blood vessels must be established promptly to supply the growing tissue with nutrients, remove cellular waste, and transport new leukocytes to the area. Fibroblasts, the primary cells responsible for depositing granulation tissue, rely on oxygen to proliferate and lay down the new extracellular matrix. During angiogenesis, endothelial cells rapidly grow into the tissue from pre-existing, intact blood vessels. These new vessels branch out systematically and form connections, or anastomoses, with other vessels to create a functional vascular network.
